original_question: Let C1,..., Cn be(left or right) cosets of a finite group G such that U:= C1 ∪ · · · ∪ Cn is not G. Is it always true that |G \ U | ⩾ |G|/2n? Affirmative answers are known in some special cases(B. Sambale, M. Tărnăuceanu, J. Algebraic Combin., 55(2022), 979–987).
target_in_paper: Open Problem 21.115 in the section "New Problems (21st issue, 2026)".
correct_elements: Your draft already captures the right ambient setting (a finite group), the right objects (a union of n left/right cosets), the proper-union hypothesis U ≠ G, and the intended lower bound for the uncovered set. In substance, it is very close to Problem 21.115.
missing_details: The denominator should be written unambiguously as 2^n rather than 2n.
The universal quantifiers should be explicit: the question is for every positive integer n, every finite group G, and every such family of cosets.
Each C_i should be specified as a left or right coset of some subgroup H_i ≤ G; the subgroups may depend on i.
It should be explicit that U := C_1 ∪ ··· ∪ C_n is a proper subset of G.
No extra assumptions such as normality, abelianness, nilpotence, or all cosets coming from the same subgroup should be added.
refined_question: For every positive integer n, every finite group G, and every family C_1, ..., C_n of subsets of G such that each C_i is either a left coset or a right coset of some subgroup H_i ≤ G, if U := C_1 ∪ ··· ∪ C_n is a proper subset of G, must one always have |G ∖ U| ≥ |G|/2^n?
justification: The draft is targeting the notebook’s open Problem 21.115 directly, rather than a broader neighboring statement. The problem appears exactly in the "New Problems (21st issue, 2026)" section and asks whether a proper union of n cosets in a finite group must leave at least a 2^{-n} fraction of the group uncovered. The paper gives essentially no additional local notation beyond U := C_1 ∪ ··· ∪ C_n and the condition U ≠ G, so the main sharpening needed is to make the quantifiers and the coset hypothesis fully explicit and to remove the ambiguity in the denominator.
